Lobbyists as an influence on Parliament's law making
Advantage: political influence gives government democratic mandate to legislate
Disadvantage: political influence can lead to manifesto pledges being abandoned or hasty legislation
Advantage: public opinion can prompt Parliament to respond quickly to public concern (e.g. Dangerous Dogs Act)
Disadvantage: public opinion is hard to gauge accurately and may not represent the whole population
Advantage: media raises awareness of issues and can trigger law reform campaigns
Disadvantage: media can be biased, sensationalist or owned by narrow interests distorting the agenda
Advantage: pressure groups provide expertise and represent minority/specialist interests
Disadvantage: pressure groups may conflict with each other or use disruptive tactics undermining legitimacy
Advantage: lobbyists give MPs detailed technical information to inform debate
Disadvantage: lobbying can give disproportionate influence to wealthy or well-connected interests
Green Paper: initial consultation document setting out proposals for reform
White Paper: firm government proposals for legislation following consultation
Public Bill: proposed law of general application (government or backbench)
Private Member's Bill: Bill introduced by a backbench MP via ballot, ten-minute rule or presentation
Private Bill: legislation affecting only a specific individual, organisation or locality
Hybrid Bill: Bill combining features of public and private Bills
First Reading: formal introduction of the Bill and publication of its title
Second Reading: full debate and vote on the main principles of the Bill
Committee Stage: detailed clause-by-clause examination and amendment by a committee
Report Stage: committee amendments reported back to and voted on by the House
Third Reading: final vote on the Bill as amended, with debate normally limited
Bill passes through the same stages in the other House
'Ping pong': Bill passed back and forth between Commons and Lords until agreement reached on amendments
Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949: Commons can override Lords' delay after set time limits
Royal Assent: the Crown's formal approval turning a Bill into an Act of Parliament
Role of the Crown in the legislative process: State Opening and Royal Assent as constitutional formalities
Advantage: multiple stages in both Houses allow thorough scrutiny and debate of proposals
Advantage: process is democratic as it involves elected representatives (Commons) voting on the Bill
Advantage: House of Lords provides independent expertise and revision free from constituency pressure
Advantage: Green/White Paper consultation allows input from interested parties before a Bill is drafted
Disadvantage: the legislative process is lengthy and can delay urgently needed law
Disadvantage: party whip system can limit genuine free debate and independent voting by MPs
Disadvantage: most Private Members' Bills fail due to lack of parliamentary time
Disadvantage: unelected House of Lords can delay or amend Bills passed by the elected Commons
Disadvantage: programme/guillotine motions can restrict time for scrutiny of complex Bills
Delegated legislation: law made by a body other than Parliament under authority conferred by a parent/enabling Act
Orders in Council: delegated legislation made by the Privy Council, often used in emergencies or to transfer EU-derived powers
Statutory Instruments: delegated legislation made by government ministers/departments to implement or supplement Acts
By-laws: delegated legislation made by local authorities or public bodies for their local area or specific undertaking
Reason for delegated legislation: lack of parliamentary time to deal with technical/local detail
Reason for delegated legislation: allows use of technical expertise Parliament itself lacks
Reason for delegated legislation: enables quick law making/updating, including in emergencies
Reason for delegated legislation: allows local knowledge to be applied to local issues (by-laws)
Reason for delegated legislation: allows future/unforeseen detailed changes without needing a new Act
Parliamentary control: affirmative resolution procedure requiring positive parliamentary approval of an SI
Parliamentary control: negative resolution procedure allowing an SI to become law unless Parliament objects within a set period
Parliamentary control: Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments scrutinises SIs on technical grounds (e.g. vires, clarity)
Parliamentary control: the enabling/parent Act itself defines and limits the scope of delegated power granted
Parliamentary control: Parliament can repeal the parent Act, removing the delegated power altogether
Judicial control: ultra vires - delegated legislation can be challenged as beyond the powers granted by the parent Act
Judicial control: procedural ultra vires - failure to follow procedure required by the parent Act (Aylesbury Mushrooms 1972)
Judicial control: substantive ultra vires - the delegated legislation itself goes beyond the powers granted (A-G v Fulham Corporation 1921)
Judicial control: unreasonableness/Wednesbury unreasonableness as a ground of challenge (Wednesbury Corporation 1948)
Judicial control: judicial review as the procedure by which delegated legislation is challenged in the courts
Effectiveness of parliamentary controls: limited due to time pressure, negative resolution rarely debated, committee lacks power to amend
Effectiveness of judicial controls: judicial review is effective but only used after challenge is brought, costly and limited to those with standing
Advantage of delegated legislation: saves parliamentary time for major policy debate
Advantage of delegated legislation: uses specialist/technical expertise unavailable to MPs generally
Advantage of delegated legislation: can be made or amended quickly, useful in emergencies or fast-changing areas
Advantage of delegated legislation: flexible - easier to amend/update than a full Act of Parliament
Advantage of delegated legislation: by-laws allow decisions suited to local conditions/needs
Disadvantage of delegated legislation: law made by unelected bodies raises democratic deficit concerns
Disadvantage of delegated legislation: sub-delegation of law-making power obscures accountability for the rules made
Disadvantage of delegated legislation: huge volume makes it hard for Parliament and the public to keep track of/scrutinise
Disadvantage of delegated legislation: controls (parliamentary and judicial) are limited in practice, risking unchecked law making
Literal rule: words of a statute given their plain, ordinary, grammatical meaning even if the result seems unjust (Whiteley v Chappell 1868; LNER v Berriman 1946)
Golden rule: literal meaning applied unless it produces an absurd result, which the court then modifies (narrow approach: R v Allen 1872; wide approach: Re Sigsworth 1935)
Mischief rule: court looks at the gap/mischief the statute was passed to remedy and interprets to suppress it (Heydon's Case 1584; Smith v Hughes 1960)
Purposive approach: court looks beyond the mischief to give effect to the wider purpose/intention behind the legislation (Jones v Tower Boot Co 1997; R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State 2003)
Advantage of literal rule: respects parliamentary sovereignty and separation of powers by not letting judges legislate
Advantage of literal rule: promotes certainty and predictability as words are given fixed ordinary meaning
Disadvantage of literal rule: can produce absurd or unjust outcomes, as in LNER v Berriman
Disadvantage of literal rule: assumes every statute can be drafted with perfect precision, which is unrealistic given the limits of language
Advantage of golden rule: avoids the worst absurdities of the literal rule while respecting the words used (Re Sigsworth)
Disadvantage of golden rule: only usable in limited absurdity cases, providing no coherent method otherwise
Disadvantage of golden rule: no fixed test for what counts as 'absurd', making outcomes unpredictable and dependent on individual judges
Advantage of mischief rule: allows judges to close the gap Parliament intended to address, promoting justice
Advantage of mischief rule: flexible, allowing law to adapt to situations Parliament may not have foreseen
Disadvantage of mischief rule: creates uncertainty as judges may go beyond genuine parliamentary intention
Disadvantage of mischief rule: risks unelected judges effectively making law, undermining separation of powers
Advantage of purposive approach: gives effect to the broader intention of Parliament, suiting a modern/EU-influenced legal system
Advantage of purposive approach: enables statutes to be applied sensibly to situations unforeseen at the time of drafting
Disadvantage of purposive approach: gives judges wide discretion to decide what Parliament 'must have intended', risking judicial law making
Disadvantage of purposive approach: purpose can be difficult to identify with certainty, reducing predictability
Rule of language: ejusdem generis - general words following specific words are limited to the same category (Powell v Kempton Park 1899)
Rule of language: expressio unius est exclusio alterius - express mention of one thing excludes others not mentioned
Rule of language: noscitur a sociis - a word takes its meaning from the words surrounding it
Intrinsic aids: sources within the Act itself, e.g. long/short title, preamble, definition sections, schedules
Extrinsic aid: dictionaries of the time used to establish the ordinary meaning of a word
Extrinsic aid: Hansard (parliamentary debates), usable following Pepper v Hart (1993) to clarify ambiguous legislation
Extrinsic aid: other external sources such as earlier case law, Law Commission/other reports, and dictionaries from the time of enactment
Advantage of rules of language: promote consistency and predictability by applying settled linguistic conventions
Disadvantage of rules of language: rigid application can still produce outcomes contrary to Parliament's real intention
Advantage of intrinsic aids: readily available within the Act, providing a reliable and objective source of interpretation
Advantage of Hansard as an aid: allows courts to discover the true purpose behind ambiguous wording (Pepper v Hart)
Disadvantage of Hansard as an aid: debates can be lengthy, unclear or unrepresentative of Parliament's collective intention, and searching them is costly

Impact of EU law on statutory interpretation: UK courts required to use a purposive approach to interpret law consistently with EU law/directives while EU law applied (Marleasing principle; now retained EU law post-Brexit)
Impact of Human Rights Act 1998 s.3 on statutory interpretation: legislation must be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights so far as possible, reinforcing the purposive approach
Advantage of EU/HRA influence: promotes consistent, rights-compliant and purposive interpretation across UK statutes
Disadvantage of EU/HRA influence: further increases judicial discretion and can blur the line between interpreting and making law
